Two weeks ago, the Climate Aligned Finance Act (CAFA) was reintroduced into the Senate by Senator Rosa Galvez. Through a number of legislative proposals, CAFA seeks to limit both the risks that financial institutions pose to the climate, and the risks climate change poses to Canada's financial system.

CAFA was first introduced in March of 2022, where it was endorsed by 89 investment firms, academic organizations, and environmental groups, and heralded as one of the most ambitious pieces of climate legislation currently underway. At the Toronto Climate Observatory, we looked to CAFA to help inform the recommendations of our inaugural Bay St. Climate Report (linked below). CAFA has been similarly upheld by environmental organizations and sustainable finance experts, including Environmental Defence and Shift Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health, as an amalgamation of leading thought on climate-aligned legislation in Canada.

This new version of CAFA includes most of the important sections from its first iteration, while changing some pieces that were holding it up under its first reading. In its current version, CAFA includes actions such as: 

📌 Mandating financial institutions to develop emissions reductions targets that align with climate commitments.

✅ Requiring financial institutions create climate transition plans detailing their plans to achieve these targets.

➡️ Directing federal regulators to create guidelines on transition risks and exposures for financial institutions.

🔎 Enforcing the disclosure of conflicts of interest, with regards to the fossil fuel industry, by any individual who sits on the board of a financial institution.

Our work at the Toronto Climate Observatory has shown that voluntary commitments from financial institutions are insufficient, further positioning this bill as a critical step in Canada's climate transition. As it moves forward through the legislative process, CAFA remains a benchmark piece of legislation in Canada, providing the structural rules and accountability necessary to align our financial system with climate action. 

For more information, read this summary from Environmental Defence Canada: https://lnkd.in/gY8Xx3S7 

Watch this interview with Senator Rosa Galvez: https://lnkd.in/esP78eyX 

Learn how this relates to the 2025 Federal Budget from Shift Action: https://lnkd.in/guMYwdiy 

Read our 2024 Bay St. Climate Report: https://lnkd.in/eYfsKJsC

📣 Workshop alert! Technologies: Data, tools, and infrastructures will bring to you an examination of the technical foundations that enable effective flood risk management in Southern Ontario.

🗓️ Tuesday, October 14, 2025
🕐 1 pm - 2.30 pm
👩‍💻 Open to all municipal and conservation authority staff from Southern Ontario
👥 Co-hosted by Toronto Climate Observatory & Climate Action Partnership
💌 Reach out to taneea@cs.toronto.edu for registration details

💡 What to expect:
Join us for an in-depth workshop to explore how the technologies behind our flood information systems shape who gets access to critical data — and who doesn't — from the nature of the data we collect, to the tools we use to analyze and communicate flood information. We'll examine how hydrometric networks, satellite monitoring, hydraulic modeling software, and sensor technologies work together to create flood information systems — and how these technical choices can either support or hinder equitable access to vital flood data.

🎙️ Special guest speaker:
Dr Rodrigo Costa, Assistant Professor, Systems Design Engineering, University of Waterloo

Dr Costa's research focuses on societal and environmental systems and examines how communities' physical, economic, and social systems interact to exacerbate disaster risk and further socioeconomic and racial inequalities. His goal is to inform targeted interventions to reduce disaster impacts, accelerate recovery, and ensure that all of society participates in the benefits.

Talk title: Repeated and localized flooding is an underestimated challenge for urban disaster risk management

Talk description: While large-scale disasters attract national and federal attention and assistance, localized flood events often don't qualify for external aid — despite being just as devastating for those impacted. Dr. Costa will present a methodology to evaluate long-term impacts of repeated, localized disasters, showing how a 20-year flood with no external assistance can lead to greater cumulative losses than a 100-year flood event.

🌍 Why it matters:
Together, we'll explore how today's flood data systems and modeling tools shape equity outcomes, and discuss how we might redesign data collection, processing, and dissemination systems to better serve all communities and support equitable flood risk management across Southern Ontario.

👥 Who should attend:
All municipal staff and conservation authority staff from Southern Ontario are welcome, particularly those working on flood risk management, infrastructure resilience, and climate adaptation in Southern Ontario.

📩 Interested in attending?
 Reach out to taneea@cs.toronto.edu for more details and registration.
